description: OrbitalQ, a project exploring SPHEREx infrared data through an interactive discovery platform aligned with the Planet X challenge. Experienced in full-stack development, UI/UX and agile project management. Looking for motivated collaborators interested in astronomy, astrophysics, Python, data science, scientific visualization or quantum computing to help turn scientific ideas into reality.
summary:
What changes when we look at the same patch of sky again?

OrbitalQ turns real NASA SPHEREx observations into an accessible visual exploration of the changing infrared sky. Built for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, our public web application lets users play dated image sequences, compare visits with a swipe divider, explore infrared wavelength channels, and inspect original FITS observations.

Ready-to-view fields help newcomers begin immediately, while coordinate inputs, file uploads, and official archive queries support deeper exploration. Observation dates, source links, and quality information keep the evidence within reach.

Our approach combines an inviting interface with scientific transparency: wavelength channels are distinguished from observation dates, and visible differences are treated as questions to investigate—not confirmed discoveries.

Designed for students, educators, astronomy enthusiasts, and citizen scientists, OrbitalQ lowers the barrier between complex astronomical files and meaningful visual investigation. It invites more people to explore NASA’s public data, notice possible changes, and follow their curiosity back to the source.
details:
FROM A PATCH OF SKY TO A QUESTION WORTH EXPLORING

Astronomical observations become more meaningful when people can compare them. A point of light may appear to move or change brightness between visits, but understanding that difference requires access to the images, their dates, and their scientific context.

OrbitalQ brings these elements together in a public web application developed for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Our goal is to make infrared sky exploration approachable while preserving the connection between what users see and the underlying evidence.

WHAT USERS CAN DO

• Explore prepared observation sequences for Barnard’s Star, WISE 0855−0714, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis.
• Play and pause dated visits, adjust playback speed, select individual observations, and use zoom and crosshair controls.
• Compare prepared visits with an interactive swipe divider.
• Explore wavelength channels in a built-in SPHEREx DR1 All-Sky Cube field.
• Enter sky coordinates, load public SPHEREx Level 2 FITS links, or upload compatible files.
• Query the official archive for candidate exposures and check whether their image footprints contain the requested coordinates.
• Inspect available metadata and follow links to original observations.

HOW IT WORKS

OrbitalQ has two complementary paths. Prepared sequences provide an immediate introduction to visual comparison. The FITS workspace supports closer inspection of individual observations using their original image data and metadata.

For FITS loading, Astropy reads the World Coordinate System, maps the requested right ascension and declination to image pixels, and extracts a cutout. Available observation times support chronological ordering. FLAGS and VARIANCE extensions are inspected when present, with missing or incompatible quality information reported to the user.

Live archive searches use NASA/IPAC IRSA’s SIA2 service for SPHEREx DR1 and QR3. Searches are bounded and depend on service availability. An incomplete query or failed file validation is not presented as evidence that no observations exist.

DESIGNED FOR EXPLORATION AND ACCOUNTABILITY

The interface offers a clear starting point for newcomers and progressively exposes technical details. Users can begin with a prepared field, compare visits, and then inspect source information.

We distinguish spectral exploration from temporal comparison. The cube’s channels represent infrared wavelengths; a time sequence requires separate dated observations. Differences in wavelength, detector, processing, alignment, or image quality can affect appearance.

Prepared previews include externally processed SPHEREx cutouts. Their processing provenance and applicable credits are retained alongside links to the original NASA/IPAC exposures. These previews are not presented as independently regenerated scientific measurements.

TECHNOLOGY

OrbitalQ uses Python and Streamlit for the application, Astropy for FITS and coordinate handling, NumPy for numerical operations, and Matplotlib for image rendering. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript power the embedded comparison and timeline interfaces. HTTP and remote-file libraries support access to public archive resources.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

OrbitalQ helps students, educators, astronomy enthusiasts, and citizen scientists engage with real infrared observations without first building a scientific processing pipeline. It supports visual inquiry, data literacy, and source-aware exploration.

Its creative contribution is the combination of an approachable observation journey with visible scientific context: choose a field, follow its visits, compare details, and trace the evidence.

CURRENT SCOPE AND NEXT STEPS

The current application supports visual investigation. It does not claim autonomous anomaly detection, confirmed discoveries, or scientifically validated measurements of motion or variability.

Priorities for further development include more independently validated observation sequences, stronger archive reliability, image-registration checks, and uncertainty-aware measurements. Any future candidate-ranking system should explain its evidence and limitations rather than present a score as a discovery probability.

Source code: https://github.com/SouBeatrizKaroline/NasaSpaceApp_OrbitalQ
